title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 12
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: The Colour That Started an Industry
passages.text:
A. Before the middle of the nineteenth century, every colour applied to cloth came from a living thing or from the ground. Reds from insects and roots, blues from plants, purples from a shellfish so laborious to process that the colour signified rank by cost alone. Dyeing was accordingly a trade of scarcity, in which the palette available to a manufacturer was set by agriculture and by trade routes rather than by chemistry.

B. The first synthetic dye was produced by accident during an attempt to make something else. A student working on the synthesis of a medicine obtained instead a dark residue that yielded an intense purple when treated with alcohol. The significant part of the episode is not the accident, which is common in laboratories, but what followed: the student recognised a commercial application, left academic work, and built a factory. Recognition rather than discovery is what made the event historically consequential.

C. What the discovery revealed was that a family of useful compounds could be built from coal tar, a waste product of gas manufacture available in quantity and effectively free. An industry therefore emerged not from a shortage being solved but from a residue finding a use, and the location of that industry followed the availability of the residue, the chemists trained to work with it, and the universities producing them.

D. The competitive advantage proved to lie in trained personnel rather than in any individual product. Nations whose universities produced large numbers of research chemists dominated the sector within a generation, and firms in those countries established the pattern of the industrial research laboratory: a permanent staff employed to generate new compounds rather than to improve existing production. This organisational form, more than any dye, is the lasting legacy of the period.

E. Consequences reached well beyond textiles, and by a route that was not planned. Compounds developed to stain fabric were found to stain biological tissue selectively, and selective staining made cell structures visible under the microscope for the first time. The same chemistry that coloured cloth therefore founded modern histology, and the observation that a dye which binds selectively to a bacterium might also harm it selectively became the reasoning that produced the first synthetic antibacterial drugs.

F. The environmental record of the industry has been poor from the outset and is improving unevenly. Dye manufacture and application are water-intensive and generate effluent that is highly coloured, chemically complex and difficult to treat, and production has repeatedly relocated toward jurisdictions where discharge is least constrained. This is not a technical limitation — treatment methods exist and work — but a consequence of who bears the cost, which is the same structure that appears wherever a cheap process externalises a expensive consequence.

passages.title: After the Whaling
passages.text:
Commercial whaling in the twentieth century removed the great whales at a scale that is difficult to convey without figures, and the figures are extraordinary: several populations were reduced by more than ninety per cent, and some by considerably more. The cessation of most commercial hunting in the second half of the century therefore created something rare in ecology — a large-scale removal followed by a large-scale release, observed with reasonable data.

Recovery has been real and strikingly uneven. Some populations have increased at rates close to the biological maximum for their species and now approach pre-whaling estimates. Others, subject to the same protection for the same period, have barely moved. The explanation is not a single factor but a set: how small the population became, whether breeding groups remained intact, the availability of prey, and continuing pressures unrelated to hunting such as ship strike, entanglement in fishing gear and noise.

Population size at the bottom matters more than the proportion removed, which is a distinction frequently blurred. A population reduced by ninety-five per cent from a very large starting number may retain enough individuals and enough genetic variation to rebuild; one reduced by the same proportion from a smaller base may fall below the level at which individuals reliably find one another to breed. Some remnant populations are estimated in the low hundreds, and for these the arithmetic of recovery is different in kind rather than in degree.

The ecological consequences of removal turned out to be less predictable than expected. The straightforward assumption was that removing enormous consumers would leave more prey for everything else. What has been observed in several systems is closer to the reverse, because whales moving between depths and across latitudes transport nutrients that would otherwise sink, and their waste fertilises surface waters where photosynthesis occurs. The whale is a consumer and also a pump, and removing the pump reduced the productivity that supported the prey.

This finding is genuine and has been overextended. The quantitative contribution of whales to ocean productivity is uncertain, estimates vary by an order of magnitude, and the systems studied are few. That whales redistribute nutrients is established; that restoring whale populations would produce a specified increase in fisheries or carbon uptake is a modelled projection with wide bounds, and it is presented in advocacy with a confidence the underlying work does not carry.

The current threats are also not the historical one, which complicates the politics. Ship strike and entanglement kill whales in numbers that matter for slow-recovering populations, and both are addressable by measures — rerouting shipping lanes, speed restrictions in known aggregation areas, modified fishing gear — that are undramatic, locally costly and demonstrably effective. Protection now means logistics rather than prohibition, which mobilises far less public attention than a hunting ban did.

passages.title: Why Organisations Repeat Their Accidents
passages.text:
Investigations into serious accidents in complex organisations reach conclusions with a consistency that is itself informative. The same categories of finding recur across industries that share no technology: warnings that were raised and not escalated, procedures that had drifted from documented practice, production pressure that made the safe option the slow one, and a recommendation from a previous incident that was accepted and not implemented.

The last of these is the most uncomfortable. Organisations that have suffered a serious event typically commission a thorough investigation, accept its findings and publish an action plan — and a substantial proportion of subsequent events are found to involve exactly the failure the earlier plan addressed. The failure is not of analysis but of implementation, and the interval between them is where attention leaves. An action plan competes for resources with everything else once the event is no longer recent, and it competes badly, because its benefit is the absence of something.

Normalisation of deviance describes the mechanism most frequently identified. A procedure is departed from, nothing happens, and the departure becomes the informal standard; it is departed from further, nothing happens again, and the new standard shifts. Each step is small and each is supported by evidence — the evidence being that the previous step caused no harm. By the time an event occurs, the practice that produced it has been normal for years, which is why investigations so often find that the immediate cause was routine.

Reporting systems fail in a pattern that is well documented and slow to correct. Staff report readily where reports produce visible change and where the reporter is protected; they stop reporting where reports disappear into a system that returns nothing. Volume of reports is therefore a poor safety indicator and is widely used as one, with the perverse result that a falling report count can be presented as improvement when it may indicate the opposite. Organisations that measure the proportion of reports receiving a substantive response learn more than those counting submissions.

The role of individual blame is where practice diverges most sharply from evidence. Identifying a responsible person is quick, satisfying and organisationally convenient, and it reliably suppresses the information the organisation needs, because people do not report what may be used against them. Systems that separate accountability for wilful violation from the reporting of error obtain more information and are harder to operate, since the boundary between the two is genuinely difficult to draw and must be drawn by someone.

What distinguishes organisations with better records is not the absence of these problems but the presence of arrangements that assume them. Independent safety functions that do not report to production management, mandatory review of whether previous recommendations were implemented, and deliberate examination of near misses rather than only of events all address the failure modes directly. None is novel, and their adoption remains partial for the same reason the original recommendations went unimplemented: they cost something now against a benefit that is invisible when it works.
